newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Northern Uzbek forces head for Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Northern Uzbek forces head for Afghan war.

text.p: Powerful Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum sent tanks, artillery and infantry towards Afghanistan's latest battle on Thursday but Kabul's Taleban rulers said he had assured them he would stay out of it.

Dostum, who has so far remained on the sidelines of the war between the purist Islamic Taleban and the government they drove from Kabul three weeks ago, sent in his forces a day after talks with the capital's new rulers.

The Taleban acting Information Minister, Amir Khan Mutaqi, said the delegation returned satisfied with the talks in Dostum's capital at Mazar-i-Sharif north of the Hindu Kush and that he had given assurances he would not join in the war.
He said one aim of the Pakistani-brokered talks was to persuade Dostum not to back the military chief of the ousted government, Ahmad Shah Masood, in his thrust south towards Kabul.
The negotiations followed the Uzbek chief's agreement last week to help Masood unless the Taleban stopped fighting.

The two men and Shia Moslem leader Karim Khalili agreed to set up an Afghan Defence Council, but his talks with the Taleban led to suspicions among Afghan-watchers that Dostum's commitment was less than firm.
"The Northern Movement (Dostum) has given us assurances. We are satisfied with them," Mutaqi said after Dostum sent his men south.
"If he does join in the fighting, it will be his decision," Mutaqi said without elaboration.
He told Reuters a Dostum delegation was expected in the near future in Kandahar, the Taleban headquarters, for further talks.

But Dostum General Abdul Majid Ruzi made plain on Friday the Uzbeks intended to join Masood, who is both a former ally and former enemy, in the drive on Kabul, Reuters correspondent Kurt Schork reported from Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush.

"As you know, the (Afghan Defence) Council decided that if there was an atttack, all forces would come together and we would insert our troops and our tanks and our artillery into the line and we have," Ruzi said.

His men appeared eager for battle. "We came from Salang and we're going to Kabul. We're going to bash the Taleban today. There are 5,000 of us coming," said one Uzbek soldier repairing a tank south of Jabal os-Siraj.
Afghan-watchers regard Dostum, who has perhaps the most powerful single fighting force in Afghanistan, as the key to the country's latest battle for power.

In the past few days, the largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban have sent heavy reinforcements into the battle on the plain north of Kabul and pushed Masood back after losing Jabal os-Siraj and the nearby town of Charikar to a counter-attack.

But if Dostum's troops do plunge into the battle now raging around Bagram junction, where the main road north meets the road running past the government's main air base just south of Charikar, the Taleban could have a torrid time.
The two sides shelled each other heavily around the junction, some 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, but neither seemed to have the upper hand, witnesses said.

On Wednesday, the Taleban rejected a Masood ultimatum to quit Kabul or face bloodshed, saying there were enough Taleban to defend the city on which they imposed Islam's stern Sharia law shortly after taking it.
But they might not be able to hold it against both Dostum and Masood, whose spokesman billed Dostum's deployment as a victory.
